summary: The note is a clipped Wikipedia article on incinerator bottom ash (IBA), the agglomerated ash discharged from the moving grate of municipal incinerators. It explains that processed IBA can be used as an aggregate in bulk fill and lightweight blocks, and that unused material may be sent elsewhere when no local market exists. It also covers metal recovery from the ash and health and safety guidance on using IBA aggregates. Much of the page is navigation and template boilerplate, which was ignored.
one_line: Overview of incinerator bottom ash: its production in municipal incinerators, reuse as processed aggregate, metal recovery, and safety guidance.
key_facts: Incinerator bottom ash (IBA) is agglomerated ash produced in the lower part of an oven or kiln.
IBA is discharged from the moving grate of municipal incinerators.
Once IBA is processed by removing contaminants, it can be used as an aggregate, termed IBA aggregate or processed IBA.
Listed aggregate uses of IBA include bulk fill and lightweight blocks.
If there are no local markets for IBA, the material is handled through an alternative route described in the note.
Between 5-15% of the bottom ash is made up of ferrous metals.
Non-ferrous (NFe) metals make up 10-30% of IBA, and they are not systematically recovered in any processing plants.
On average, 63 kg of ferrous materials are removed from a single tonne of ash.
The Health and Safety Executive updated its guidelines to suggest IBA aggregates can only be poured in open air.
The updated Health and Safety Executive guidance says IBA aggregates should be used only in well ventilated areas.
The guidance also states IBA aggregates should not be used during setting.
